mcqs.q: Diabetes mellitus is characterised by:
mcqs.explain: DM is a metabolic disorder of hyperglycaemia, causing capillary thickening and vascular complications (retinopathy, neuropathy, atherosclerosis).

mcqs.q: Type 1 diabetes is:
mcqs.explain: Type 1 is insulin-dependent; Type 2 is non-insulin dependent; gestational diabetes occurs in pregnancy.

mcqs.q: The classic triad of diabetes symptoms is:
mcqs.explain: The classic symptoms are polyuria (excess urine), polydipsia (excess thirst) and polyphagia (excess hunger), plus fatigue, weight loss and blurred vision.

mcqs.q: Oral manifestations of diabetes include:
opts: Xerostomia, periodontitis, candidiasis and delayed healing
mcqs.explain: Diabetics show increased xerostomia, gingivitis/periodontitis, candidiasis, burning mouth and delayed wound healing.

mcqs.q: Insulin is synthesised in the:
opts: β cells of the pancreatic islets
mcqs.explain: Insulin is made in the β cells of the pancreatic islets; its main action is to lower blood glucose (hypoglycaemia).

mcqs.q: Which are rapid-acting insulins?
mcqs.explain: Insulin lispro, aspart and glulisine have a more rapid, predictable onset and shorter duration than regular insulin.

mcqs.q: Metformin (a biguanide) lowers glucose mainly by:
mcqs.explain: Metformin reduces glucose production by the liver; its rare but serious side effect is lactic acidosis.

mcqs.q: Sulfonylureas such as glipizide act by:
opts: Stimulating insulin secretion (risk of hypoglycaemia/weight gain)
mcqs.explain: Sulfonylureas (glipizide) stimulate insulin secretion; side effects include hypoglycaemia and weight gain.

mcqs.q: SGLT-2 inhibitors (e.g. empagliflozin) lower glucose by:
opts: Promoting glucose excretion in the urine
mcqs.explain: SGLT-2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption, promoting urinary glucose loss.

mcqs.q: The most frequent and serious reaction to insulin therapy is:
mcqs.explain: Hypoglycaemia is the most frequent and potentially most serious insulin reaction — risky if a meal is missed after a dental procedure.

mcqs.q: A diabetic patient on insulin who misses a meal after a dental procedure is at risk of:
mcqs.explain: Missing a meal (or a large dose/exercise) can precipitate hypoglycaemia: sweating, tremor, palpitations, then confusion and possibly seizures.

mcqs.q: A glucometer reading indicating hypoglycaemia is:
mcqs.explain: Blood glucose ≤70 mg/dL indicates hypoglycaemia, requiring immediate treatment.

mcqs.q: First-line treatment of a CONSCIOUS hypoglycaemic dental patient is to:
mcqs.explain: A conscious hypoglycaemic patient should be given 15–20 g of oral carbohydrate; recheck glucose afterwards.

mcqs.q: If a hypoglycaemic dental patient is UNCONSCIOUS, the appropriate drug is:
mcqs.explain: An unconscious patient cannot eat/drink — injectable glucagon signals the liver to release glucose while emergency help is summoned.

mcqs.q: Ideal scheduling for a controlled diabetic dental patient is:
opts: Morning appointments, ensuring they do not miss a meal
mcqs.explain: Morning appointments suit controlled diabetics; avoid hypoglycaemia by ensuring the patient eats normally, and give prophylactic antibiotics if poorly controlled.

mcqs.q: Peptic ulcers are mucosal lesions caused by:
opts: The action of acid and pepsin
mcqs.explain: Peptic ulcers result from acid and pepsin damaging the gastric/duodenal mucosa; causes include H. pylori, NSAIDs and stress/smoking.

mcqs.q: A major bacterial cause of peptic ulcers is:
mcqs.explain: Helicobacter pylori infection is a major cause of peptic ulcers; NSAID use is another key cause.

mcqs.q: Proton pump inhibitors (e.g. omeprazole) work by:
opts: Irreversibly inhibiting the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase of gastric parietal cells
mcqs.explain: PPIs irreversibly inhibit the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase (proton pump), giving strong acid suppression; long-term use risks B12 deficiency.

mcqs.q: Famotidine reduces gastric acid by:
mcqs.explain: Famotidine is an H2-receptor antagonist, giving moderate acid suppression (ranitidine was withdrawn in many regions).

mcqs.q: Eradication of H. pylori typically uses:
opts: Triple therapy: a PPI plus two antibiotics
mcqs.explain: H. pylori is eradicated with triple therapy (PPI + 2 antibiotics, e.g. amoxicillin + metronidazole) or quadruple therapy (adding bismuth).

mcqs.q: Which agent is a prostaglandin analogue used for NSAID-induced ulcers?
mcqs.explain: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin analogue that enhances mucus/bicarbonate secretion, used to prevent/treat NSAID-induced ulcers; sucralfate forms a protective barrier.

mcqs.q: Antacids such as aluminium and magnesium hydroxide:
opts: Neutralize stomach acid (Al → constipation, Mg → diarrhoea)
mcqs.explain: Antacids neutralize acid for rapid symptom relief; aluminium causes constipation and magnesium causes diarrhoea.

mcqs.q: A dental drug-interaction concern with PPIs is that they may:
opts: Reduce the absorption of antifungal drugs
mcqs.explain: By raising gastric pH, PPIs can interfere with the absorption of some antifungals; antibiotics for H. pylori may cause oral candidiasis.

mcqs.q: Why give prophylactic antibiotics to some diabetic dental patients?
opts: Poorly-controlled diabetics have impaired healing and higher infection risk
mcqs.explain: Poorly-controlled diabetes impairs healing and raises infection risk, so prophylactic antibiotics may be indicated for dental procedures.

saqs.q: Classify diabetes mellitus and give its classic symptoms.
saqs.a: Type 1 (insulin-dependent), Type 2 (non-insulin), gestational. Symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia (+ fatigue, weight loss, blurred vision).

saqs.q: Match each oral antidiabetic class to its mechanism: metformin, glipizide, empagliflozin.
saqs.a: Metformin (biguanide) → ↓ hepatic glucose; glipizide (sulfonylurea) → ↑ insulin secretion; empagliflozin (SGLT-2) → ↑ urinary glucose.

saqs.q: Describe the recognition and treatment of hypoglycaemia in the dental chair.
saqs.a: Glucose ≤70 mg/dL with sweating/tremor/confusion. Conscious: 15–20 g oral carbohydrate. Unconscious: injectable glucagon + emergency help.

saqs.q: List dental management points for the diabetic patient.
saqs.a: Morning appointments, don't miss meals, prophylactic antibiotics if poorly controlled, treat periodontitis, control glucose before major procedures.

saqs.q: List the causes of peptic ulcer.
saqs.a: Helicobacter pylori, NSAIDs, and stress/smoking/alcohol — acid and pepsin damage the mucosa.
PPIs (omeprazole) irreversibly inhibit the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase — strong acid suppression. H2-antagonists (famotidine) block H2 receptors — moderate suppression.

saqs.q: How is H. pylori eradicated, and what dental concerns arise from ulcer drugs?
saqs.a: Triple therapy (PPI + 2 antibiotics) or quadruple (+ bismuth). Dental: PPIs reduce antifungal absorption; antibiotics → candidiasis; avoid NSAIDs.
